# Block 5: Priors {.unnumbered} *Roughly 30 minutes. Part B is arithmetic a child could do and most doctors cannot. Do it before you read Part C.* ## Part A: the assay You want to say "there is a 95% probability the true mean is in my interval". To be entitled to it you need one ingredient you did not have. The cleanest way to see what that ingredient is has nothing to do with beans. It is an eDNA survey. You are surveying ponds for a rare protected species. The assay is good: - **Sensitivity 90%.** If the species is there, you detect it nine times in ten. - **False positive rate 5%.** If it is absent, you get a spurious positive one time in twenty. You sample a pond. **It tests positive.** **What is the probability the species is there?** Commit to a number before you scroll. Nearest whole per cent. % ## Part B: the count Most people say something in the eighties or nineties. Here is the arithmetic. The only trick is that we will not use a single percentage. We will count ponds. `edna_table()` is in `R/beans.R`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} #' Natural frequency table for an eDNA assay #' #' @param ponds Numeric. How many ponds to imagine. Default 1000. #' @param prevalence Numeric in (0, 1). Proportion of ponds holding the species. #' @param sensitivity Numeric in (0, 1). P(positive | species present). #' @param false_positive_rate Numeric in (0, 1). P(positive | species absent). #' @return A tibble of counts, never percentages. edna_table <- function(ponds = 1000, prevalence = 0.02, sensitivity = 0.90, false_positive_rate = 0.05) { present <- ponds * prevalence absent <- ponds - present tibble::tibble( truth = c("Species present", "Species absent"), n_ponds = c(present, absent), test_positive = c(present * sensitivity, absent * false_positive_rate), test_negative = c(present * (1 - sensitivity), absent * (1 - false_positive_rate)) ) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} edna_table() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|truth | n_ponds| test_positive| test_negative| |:---------------|-------:|-------------:|-------------:| |Species present | 20| 18| 2| |Species absent | 980| 49| 931|
::: ::: Read it out loud: - Of **1000** ponds, **20** hold the species. It is rare. That is why it is protected. - Of those 20, the assay detects **18**. - Of the **980** without it, **49** test positive anyway. - Positives total **18 + 49 = 67**. - Of those 67 positives, **18** actually have the species. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} prob_present_given_positive(prevalence = 0.02) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.2686567 ``` ::: ::: **About 27%.** A 90% sensitive assay, a 5% false positive rate, a positive result in hand, and it remains **more likely than not that the pond is empty**. The reason is the 980. The species is rare, so there are so many empty ponds that even a 5% error rate on them produces more false positives than there are true ones to find. :::{.callout-note} ## Why counts, and not the formula The count version is not a teaching indulgence. It measurably works better. McDowell and Jacobs [@mcdowell2017] meta-analysed this literature: roughly **4%** of people solve problems of this shape when the information arrives as conditional probabilities, against roughly **24%** when it arrives as natural frequencies. Visual aids improved things further. Read that honestly, though. 24% is a sixfold improvement on a catastrophic baseline, and it still means three-quarters get it wrong. The format helps. It does not rescue you from thinking. The original demonstration is Gigerenzer and Hoffrage [@gigerenzer1995]. Its companion finding is the one to remember: 24 experienced physicians, including heads of department, were given a prevalence, a sensitivity and a false positive rate and asked what a positive screening result meant. Their answers ranged from **1% to 99%**. ::: ## Part C: now change one thing Same assay. Same positive result. But this time the pond is in known good habitat, where roughly half of ponds are occupied. **Before you run it:** what happens to the answer? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} edna_table(prevalence = 0.50) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|truth | n_ponds| test_positive| test_negative| |:---------------|-------:|-------------:|-------------:| |Species present | 500| 450| 50| |Species absent | 500| 25| 475|
::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} prob_present_given_positive(prevalence = 0.50) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.9473684 ``` ::: ::: **About 95%.** :::{.callout-important} ## Stop here Same assay. Same result. **27% against 95%.** The data did not change. Not one thing about the measurement changed. What changed is what you believed **before** you took the measurement. That is a **prior**, and it is not a philosophical decoration you can decline. It was doing the work all along. In the first case it was doing 68 percentage points of work. ::: ### The whole picture ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble(prior = seq(0.001, 0.999, length.out = 500)) |> mutate(posterior = prob_present_given_positive(prior)) |> ggplot(aes(x = prior, y = posterior)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, colour = colorspace::qualitative_hcl(1, palette = "Dark 3")) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1)) + labs( x = "Prior probability the species is present", y = "Posterior probability, given a positive test" ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Posterior probability that the species is present, given one positive test, against the prior probability. Assay characteristics are identical throughout: sensitivity 90%, false positive rate 5%. The dashed line marks where a positive test leaves the question even.](05-bayes-and-priors_files/figure-html/fig-prior-curve-1.png){#fig-prior-curve fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: One curve, one assay, every possible answer from near zero to near one. Pick your prior and read off your conclusion. If you find that alarming, good. Keep reading. ## Part D: the vocabulary, arrived at rather than announced - **Prior:** what you believed before the data. Here, the prevalence. - **Likelihood:** what the data do. Here, the assay characteristics. - **Posterior:** what you believe after. The prior, updated by the data. And a second definition of probability, incompatible with the one you pulled off the wall in Block 2. Not a long-run frequency, but a **degree of belief**, which can attach to a one-off event, to a hypothesis, or to a parameter. Which is exactly what you wanted in Block 4. ## Part E: back to your interval The reason you cannot say "95% probability the true mean is in my interval" is now sayable in one line. That is a statement about the **parameter given the data**. It is a posterior. Posteriors require priors. You did not supply one. A Bayesian would. They would put a probability distribution over mean bean mass before weighing anything, update it with your ten beans, and hand you a **credible interval**, about which statement 4 is *true*. The 95% would be a degree of belief about the parameter, exactly as your instinct demanded. :::{.callout-warning} ## The inversion, three times - **eDNA:** P(positive | present) is not P(present | positive). 90% against 27%. - **Your interval:** P(interval like mine | true mean is X) is not P(true mean is X | my interval). - **Next week:** P(data like mine | null is true) is not P(null is true | my data). That is the p-value, and it is the same error a third time. One inversion. Three costumes. If you have it here, you have all three. ::: ## Part F: so why are we not all Bayesians? Look at @fig-prior-curve again. The prior did 68 points of work. In the eDNA case that is fine: prevalence is a real, measurable quantity, and somebody has surveyed those ponds. Your prior **is** data. Now suppose nobody has surveyed the ponds. You need a prior anyway, because the machinery does not run without one. So you make one up. And your posterior, that beautifully interpretable number, is now **partly made up**, in a proportion nobody can see from the outside. That is the frequentist objection, and it is not a foolish one: > Refuse to supply a prior. Say only what the data support. The price is that you can never make the statement you actually want, and you will spend your career correcting people who think you have. Pay it. :::{.callout-note} ## Where this module goes, and why **We are doing frequentist statistics for the next ten weeks.** Not because the argument is settled. It is not. Serious people have been on both sides of it for a century. Because the literature you are about to read, review and publish in is overwhelmingly frequentist, and you cannot argue with a framework you cannot use. You now know a choice was made. Most people never find out. When you meet Bayesian methods later, you will meet them as an alternative you were told about, rather than as a shock. ::: :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Five questions about priors :::: ::::{.task-container} 1. Your assay improves: sensitivity 99%, false positive rate 1%. At 2% prevalence, what does a positive mean now? Is it enough? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} prob_present_given_positive(0.02, sensitivity = 0.99, false_positive_rate = 0.01) ``` ::: 2. Which matters more for a **rare** species: raising sensitivity, or lowering the false positive rate? Use the function to find out, then explain why in one sentence. 3. Redraw @fig-prior-curve for a **common** species (prior 40% to 90%). Why is the curve so boring there, and what does that tell you about when priors matter? 4. Write `prob_absent_given_negative()`. At 2% prevalence, what does a **negative** test mean? Why is that answer so much more comfortable than the positive case, and which result should you therefore trust? 5. Somebody claims priors are unscientific because they are subjective. Using @fig-prior-curve, explain why refusing to state a prior does not mean you do not have one. :::: :::
**1.** About 67%. Better, and still not enough to bet a protected-species designation on. Rarity is punishing. **2.** **Lowering the false positive rate**, by a wide margin. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} prob_present_given_positive(0.02, sensitivity = 0.99, false_positive_rate = 0.05) # ~0.29 prob_present_given_positive(0.02, sensitivity = 0.90, false_positive_rate = 0.01) # ~0.65 ``` ::: Because sensitivity operates on the 20 occupied ponds and the false positive rate operates on the 980 empty ones. When the species is rare, almost every pond you test is empty, so almost every opportunity to be wrong is an opportunity to be wrong in that direction. Improving sensitivity from 90% to 99% wins you nine extra true positives out of 20. Cutting the false positive rate from 5% to 1% removes 39 false ones out of 980. **4.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} prob_absent_given_negative <- function(prevalence, sensitivity = 0.90, false_positive_rate = 0.05) { true_negative <- (1 - prevalence) * (1 - false_positive_rate) false_negative <- prevalence * (1 - sensitivity) true_negative / (true_negative + false_negative) } prob_absent_given_negative(0.02) # about 0.998 ``` ::: A negative is worth 99.8%. It is nearly conclusive, while the positive was nearly worthless. Same assay, same data, opposite usefulness, and the asymmetry comes entirely from the prior. When something is rare, evidence *for* it has to fight the base rate, and evidence *against* it is pushing at an open door. The lesson generalises well beyond eDNA: **the same test can be strong evidence in one direction and weak in the other**, and which is which depends on what you believed before you ran it.
